30/S0/F0.text: Sound perception occurs at three levels—social, warning, and primitive—which together give a person an overall idea of the surroundings.

30/S0/F1.text: Social-level sound perception is the level of sound perception that helps an individual carry out social interactions with other individuals.

30/S0/F2.text: Warning-level sound perception is the level of sound perception that provides an alert or warning about something, such as an event.

30/S0/F3.text: Primitive-level sound perception is the intuitive perception of naive sounds such as background noises that people mostly ignore, and it may not lead to any meaningful action by the individual.

30/S0/F4.text: Identifying the desired sound perception level helps a developer generate suitable auditory effects when generating sound effects for a virtual reality (VR) system; for example, if social-level perception is required, the developer should generate stimuli that support social-level perception rather than stimuli that typically produce primitive-level perception.

30/S1/F0.text: Psychophysics is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena that are produced by physical stimuli.

30/S1/F1.text: Psychoacoustics is a more specific area of psychophysics and is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena that are produced by acoustic stimuli or sound.

30/S1/F2.text: Stevens' power law is a result from psychophysics that characterizes the relationship between the magnitude of a physical stimulus and its perceived magnitude by the equation P = C M^x, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the original stimulus, P is the perceived magnitude, x is the exponent that relates actual magnitude to perceived magnitude, and C is a constant that depends on units.

30/S1/F3.text: The just noticeable difference (JND) is a result from psychophysics that specifies the amount of change in a stimulus that is required for subjects to perceive it as changed in at least 50 percent of trials.

30/S1/F4.text: Weber's law captures the just noticeable difference (JND), the change in magnitude that is noticeable, by representing it as delta M divided by M equals C, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the stimulus, delta M is the just noticeable difference, and C is a constant; equivalently, delta M equals M times C.

30/S1/F5.text: Weber's law and Stevens' power law are laws from psychophysics that also apply to psychoacoustics, or auditory perception, when physical stimuli are replaced by acoustic stimuli.

30/S1/F6.text: For the perceived loudness of a 3000 hertz (Hz) pure tone, the Stevens' power law exponent x is 0.67, so a much higher pressure level is perceived as only a bit louder because the exponent is less than 1.

30/S1/F7.text: For a change in a stimulus to be perceived, it must be above the just noticeable difference (JND); for it not to be perceived, it must be within or below the JND.

30/S2/F0.text: In pitch perception, the frequency of a sound wave is referred to as pitch.

30/S2/F1.text: For sound frequency, the just noticeable difference (JND) increases as frequency increases: for frequencies less than 1000 Hz, humans can detect a frequency change of less than 1 Hz; at 10,000 Hz the JND is about 100 Hz; in percentage terms, at low frequencies humans can detect frequency differences of 0.1% or less, whereas at higher frequencies a difference of at least 1% is required.

30/S3/F0.text: Sound localization is a main area of psychoacoustics that estimates the location of a sound source by hearing it.

30/S3/F1.text: Sound localization is crucial in virtual reality (VR) because it helps the user perceive the orientation and position of objects relative to the user by matching auditory and visual cues; a mismatch can break presence and cause cybersickness.

30/S3/F2.text: The minimum audible angle (MAA) is the minimum angular variation that can be detected by a human listener, obtained by applying the just noticeable difference (JND) concept to sound localization and represented in a spherical coordinate system with the listener's head as the origin.

30/S3/F3.text: The spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location has three parameters: azimuth, the angle in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the projection of the sound source direction, ranging from -180 degrees to 180 degrees; elevation, the angle between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane, ranging from -90 degrees to 90 degrees; and radius, the distance from the listener's head origin to the source.

30/S3/F4.text: The minimum audible angle (MAA) depends on both the frequency and direction of the sound source: at some frequencies and locations it can be as low as 1 degree, while at other combinations localization can be very difficult and the MAA can be extremely high.

30/S4/F0.text: Sound localization cues are either monaural, involving a single ear, or binaural, involving both ears.

30/S4/F1.text: Interaural level difference (ILD) is a binaural sound localization cue that is the difference in sound magnitude heard by each ear, with the ear without obstruction receiving a stronger sound, and the difference can indicate the direction from which the sound is coming.

30/S4/F2.text: An acoustic shadow occurs when a sound wave does not reach one ear, caused by an object in front of the sound source or by the position of the head.

30/S4/F3.text: Interaural time difference is a binaural sound localization cue from different sound arrival times at the ears; in an average human head, the ears are 21.5 centimeters apart, sound travels that distance in about 0.6 milliseconds, and this small time difference can be used to locate the source.

30/S4/F4.text: The auditory component of an extended reality (XR) system should ideally be non-stationary, moving with the user, and interactive, dependent on the listener's actions.

30/S4/F5.text: Head-related transfer functions (HRTF) model how a listener receives sound from a location in space, and this model is relevant for dealing with sound in any system, including extended reality (XR) systems.

30/S4/F6.text: Head-related transfer functions (HRTF) depend on the size and shape of the head, ears, and ear canal, and every person has a unique HRTF.

30/S4/F7.text: Because every person has a unique head-related transfer function (HRTF), it is impractical to determine individual users' HRTFs when building a system, so an HRTF for an average listener is developed and used.

30/S4/F8.text: A pair of head-related transfer functions (HRTF) for both ears can be used to synthesize binaural sound, and by generating sound effects or placing sound receivers according to the HRTF, a localization effect can be implemented in an extended reality (XR) system.
